system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2165-02-06 19:05:00 to 2165-02-07 12:10:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient, a woman with a history of Addison’s disease, hypothyroidism, hypertension, and migraines, was admitted for adrenal crisis triggered by gastroenteritis and a missed prednisone dose. She presented with hypotension, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea, and was treated with IV fluids and stress-dose steroids, which stabilized her blood pressure. Lab results revealed acute kidney injury and anion gap metabolic acidosis due to dehydration, both of which resolved with rehydration. Markedly elevated liver enzymes were attributed to unintentional acetaminophen overdose; she was treated with IV acetylcysteine for two days with improvement. A urinary tract infection caused by E. coli was identified and treated with antibiotics, transitioning to oral cefpodoxime at discharge. An EGD ruled out esophagitis. She was discharged on a prednisone taper, antibiotics, and instructions to avoid acetaminophen, with follow-up arranged.
problems: Urinary tract infection, site not specified
Other and unspecified noninfectious gastroenteritis and colitis
Aromatic analgesics, not elsewhere classified, causing adverse effects in therapeutic use
Nonspecific elevation of levels of transaminase or lactic acid dehydrogenase [LDH]

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you came in today because of weakness and diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I’ve been feeling really fatigued, like I did during my last adrenal crisis. I also had a few episodes of diarrhea, but no blood or mucus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned in the ED that you’re craving salt and feel very thirsty—those can be signs your Addison’s is flaring up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. I didn’t sleep well last night, and I think that might have triggered it. I’ve been on prednisone, but maybe I need more right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. You already got a dose of hydrocortisone in the ER, and we’re giving you IV fluids to help with dehydration. We’re treating this as an Addisonian crisis, so we’ll keep you on steroids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s reassuring. My right upper belly pain also got worse after the ultrasound earlier—was that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I saw that. The ultrasound didn’t cause harm, but it seems to have aggravated your existing pain. Your liver looks stable—no new issues. We’ll manage the pain with medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. My liver enzymes were high last time—any change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’re actually improving—ALT and AST are down from your last admission. That’s a good sign your liver is recovering from the acetaminophen effect.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I’ve been avoiding Tylenol completely since then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Smart move. We also checked your kidney function, and your creatinine was elevated—up to 1.3 from your baseline of 0.7. But it looks like it’s due to dehydration, not permanent damage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, so that’s why I feel so weak? Is it getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. With the IV fluids, your kidneys are already improving. Your latest labs show creatinine down to 0.9, which is back to normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re looking better. Your diarrhea has stopped, and you’re feeling more energetic, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, much better. I slept well last night and haven’t had any loose stools since yesterday evening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re going to switch you to oral prednisone with a taper—10 mg twice a day for two days, then gradually down. You’ll finish the taper and go back to your usual 5 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And what about the anemia? My hemoglobin was low again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your anemia is likely related to chronic disease, not acute blood loss. Iron, B12, and folate are normal. We’ll keep monitoring it, but no treatment is needed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my other meds—can I restart fludrocortisone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re adding fludrocortisone back at 0.1 mg daily after you finish the prednisone taper. It helps with salt retention, which you clearly need.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve been so thirsty. Will my anxiety meds stay the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue clonazepam as needed. Same with your thyroid, blood pressure, and GERD meds—everything else stays on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And when can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If all goes well this morning, we can discharge you by late morning. You’re stable, and your labs look good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. Your discharge instructions are ready. You’re to take the prednisone taper as scheduled, watch for worsening fatigue, fever, or diarrhea, and call if you feel lightheaded or crave salt strongly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything. I feel much more confident going home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and follow up with your endocrinologist soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again, Doctor.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of Addison’s disease, hypothyroidism, hypertension, and microscopic colitis was readmitted one week after prior discharge due to fatigue, salt craving, and diarrhea, consistent with an Addisonian crisis. She was treated with IV hydrocortisone and fluids in the emergency department, then transitioned to an oral prednisone taper. Her renal function, which was impaired due to dehydration (creatinine rising from 0.7 to 1.3), improved with rehydration and returned to baseline.
